title: Stories of the Upanishads
bigQuestion: Why do the Upanishads teach through questions and conversations, and what do their stories show about learning?

story.title: Three Nights at Death's Door
story.kicker: A boy waits three days at the house of Death, and Death offers him three wishes.
paragraphs: A father named Vajashravas is giving away his wealth in a great ritual. But the cows he gives are old and worn out. His young son, Nachiketa, notices. He worries that such a gift is not a true gift. "Father," he asks, "to whom will you give me?"

His father does not answer. Nachiketa asks again, and again. At last his father snaps in anger: "I give you to Death!" The words cannot be taken back. So Nachiketa goes to the house of Yama, the lord of death.

Yama is away. Nachiketa waits at the door for three nights with no food and no welcome. When Yama returns, he is troubled. A guest has been left hungry. To make it right, he offers the boy three wishes, one for each night.

Nachiketa's first wish is that his father will be calm and glad to see him again. His second is to learn a sacred fire ritual. His third is the hardest. "When a person dies," he asks, "some say he still is, and some say he is not. Teach me which is true."

Yama tries to talk him out of it. He offers long life, gold, horses and kingdoms instead. Nachiketa refuses every one. "Keep your horses," he says. "This is the wish I choose." This story opens the Katha Upanishad.
story.think: Why do you think Nachiketa turns down gold and kingdoms? What does his choice say about him?

lessons.title: A Boy Who Asks
lessons.mainIdea: In the Katha Upanishad, young Nachiketa questions Yama, the lord of death, about what happens after death.
reading: The Katha Upanishad opens with a problem in a ritual. Nachiketa sees his father giving away useless cows. He asks, three times, whom he himself will be given to. His father's angry answer sends him to Yama.

*Yama* is the lord of death in Hindu texts. He is not a monster. In the Katha he is a wise teacher who respects his young guest. Because he left Nachiketa waiting three nights, he offers three *boons*, or wishes.

Scholars date the Katha Upanishad to roughly the 5th century BCE or later. Its story form makes deep ideas easy to follow. Many Hindu children hear the Nachiketa story, and teachers use it to praise curiosity and courage.

words.d: the boy in the Katha Upanishad who questions Yama about death
the lord of death in Hindu texts, a wise teacher in the Katha Upanishad
a wish or gift granted by a god or sage

look.title: Three Nights, Three Wishes
look.cite: Katha Upanishad 1.1 (see F. Max Müller, SBE 15, 1884)
look.prompt: Why do you think the hardest question is the last wish?

check.q: Who is Yama in the Katha Upanishad?
choices: The lord of death and a wise teacher
check.why: Yama is the lord of death who teaches Nachiketa.

check.q: Why does Yama offer three wishes?
check.why: Yama makes up for leaving a guest three nights without food.

check.q: What is a boon?
check.why: A boon is a wish granted by a god or sage.

lessons.title: The Good and the Pleasant
lessons.mainIdea: Yama teaches that people must choose between what is pleasant and what is truly good.
reading: Yama tests Nachiketa by offering riches. When the boy refuses, Yama praises him. He says there are two paths: the *shreyas*, the good, and the *preyas*, the pleasant. The wise choose the good. The foolish choose the pleasant.

Yama then teaches about the self. He says the self is not born and does not die. It is hidden in the heart of every being. It cannot be reached just by study or cleverness, but by a mind that is calm and clear.
Many readers see Nachiketa as a model student. He cares more about the truth than about reward. Some Hindu teachers compare Yama's test to the choices students face every day, like study or play.

words.d: what is truly good, in the Katha Upanishad
what is pleasant, in the Katha Upanishad

look.title: Two Paths
look.text: The good is one thing and the pleasant is another. Both pull at a person. It goes well with the one who chooses the good; the one who chooses the pleasant misses the goal.
look.cite: Katha Upanishad 1.2.1, paraphrased (see F. Max Müller, SBE 15, 1884)
look.prompt: Give an example from school life of the good and the pleasant pulling in different directions.

check.q: What is shreyas?
check.why: Shreyas means what is truly good.

check.q: What does Yama offer Nachiketa to test him?
check.why: Yama offers wealth and long life before he agrees to teach.

check.q: According to Yama, how is the self reached?
choices: By a calm and clear mind
check.why: Yama says the self is not reached by study alone but by a calm, clear mind.

lessons.title: The Chariot
lessons.mainIdea: The Katha Upanishad compares a person to a chariot, with the self as the rider and the mind as the reins.
reading: Yama gives Nachiketa a famous picture. Think of the self as the rider in a *chariot*. The body is the chariot. Understanding is the driver. The mind is the reins. The senses are the horses.
If the driver is careless, the horses run wild. If the driver is wise and holds the reins well, the horses obey and the rider reaches the goal. Yama uses this image to teach self-control.

Readers have loved this picture for centuries. It is similar to images in Greek philosophy, such as Plato's chariot, though the two are not the same. Yoga teachers still use it to explain calming the senses.

words.d: an ancient two-wheeled cart pulled by horses
sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch

look.title: The Chariot Image
look.text: Know the self as the lord of the chariot, the body as the chariot, the intellect as the charioteer, and the mind as the reins. The senses, they say, are the horses.
look.cite: Katha Upanishad 1.3.3–4, paraphrased (see F. Max Müller, SBE 15, 1884)
look.prompt: What happens to the chariot if the horses run wild? What does that stand for?

check.q: In the chariot image, what are the horses?
check.why: The Katha says the senses are the horses.

check.q: What does the chariot image teach?
check.why: Yama uses it to teach control of the senses by a wise mind.

check.q: In the image, what are the reins?
check.why: The mind is the reins held by the driver, understanding.

lessons.title: Svetaketu Learns Again
lessons.mainIdea: In Chandogya Upanishad 6, Uddalaka teaches his proud son Svetaketu through everyday examples.
reading: Svetaketu comes home after twelve years of study, proud and sure of himself. He thinks he has learned everything. His father, *Uddalaka*, asks a simple question he cannot answer. So the real lesson begins.

Uddalaka uses things from the kitchen and the yard. He shows how many clay pots are all clay. He asks Svetaketu to split a tiny banyan seed and look inside. There seems to be nothing, yet a great tree grows from it.

Then comes the salt in the water. Each lesson ends with the refrain 'That art thou.' Many teachers point out the lesson inside the story: being proud of knowing a lot is not the same as understanding.

words.d: the father and teacher in Chandogya Upanishad 6
Uddalaka's son, who learns from his father in Chandogya 6
a line repeated at the end of each part of a poem or teaching

look.title: The Banyan Seed
look.text: Uddalaka asks his son to break open a fig seed. "What do you see?" "Nothing at all, sir." "From that fine essence you cannot see," says the father, "this great tree grows." (Chandogya 6.12)
look.prompt: What is Uddalaka teaching with the seed? How is it like the salt lesson?

check.q: How long did Svetaketu study before coming home?
check.why: Chandogya 6.1 says Svetaketu studied for twelve years.

check.q: What does Uddalaka ask his son to break open?
choices: A seed from a fig tree
check.why: In Chandogya 6.12 Svetaketu breaks open a tiny seed.

check.q: What lesson do many teachers find in Svetaketu's story?
choices: Pride in knowing is not the same as understanding
check.why: The proud son learns that real understanding goes deeper.

lessons.title: Satyakama Tells the Truth
lessons.mainIdea: In Chandogya 4.4, Satyakama honestly admits he does not know his father's name, and the teacher accepts him for his truthfulness.
reading: A boy named Satyakama wants to study with a teacher. He asks his mother about his family line. She tells him she was a servant, moved from place to place, and does not know who his father was.

Satyakama goes to the teacher, Gautama, and tells him exactly that. The teacher is moved. He says only a true Brahmin would speak so honestly. He accepts Satyakama as his student and begins to teach him.

Many Hindu teachers use this story to say that truthfulness matters more than birth. Reformers have pointed to it in arguments against caste. Others note it still uses the word Brahmin. Readers discuss both sides.

words.d: a boy in Chandogya 4.4 whose honesty wins him a teacher; his name means 'lover of truth'
always telling the truth

look.title: An Honest Answer
look.text: The teacher said to him: no one who was not a Brahmin could speak so plainly. Go, fetch fuel, friend; I shall take you as my student. You have not turned from the truth.
look.cite: Chandogya Upanishad 4.4.5, paraphrased (see F. Max Müller, SBE 1, 1879)
look.prompt: Why does the teacher accept Satyakama? What does he value most?

check.q: What does the name Satyakama mean?
check.why: Satya means truth; Satyakama is lover of truth.

check.q: Why does the teacher accept Satyakama?
choices: He told the truth about his birth
check.why: Gautama accepts him because he spoke honestly.

check.q: How have reformers used this story?
choices: To explain the Rig Veda's dates
check.why: Reformers cite it to say truthfulness matters more than birth.

lessons.title: Questioning as Learning
lessons.mainIdea: The Upanishads present asking questions as a respected way to learn.
reading: Notice how many Upanishads begin: with a question. Nachiketa asks about death. Uddalaka asks Svetaketu about the teaching that makes the unknown known. The Kena Upanishad opens: by whom is the mind sent forth?
In these texts, good students ask, and good teachers welcome it. Teachers sometimes ask back, or give a riddle, or send the student away to think. Learning is a long *inquiry*, not a single answer.

Hindu traditions call a student who seeks this knowledge a jijnasu, one who wishes to know. The Brahma Sutras begin with the words 'Now, therefore, the desire to know Brahman.' Many teachers today encourage students to bring hard questions.

words.d: a careful search for knowledge by asking questions
a seeker; one who wishes to know

look.title: Openings
look.text: Katha: a boy asks what happens after death. Kena: 'By whom is the mind sent forth?' Brahma Sutras: 'Now, therefore, the desire to know Brahman.' Chandogya 6: 'Have you asked for that teaching?'
look.prompt: What do these openings have in common? What does that suggest about how these texts see learning?

check.q: How does the Kena Upanishad begin?
choices: With a question about the mind
check.why: The Kena opens by asking by whom the mind is sent forth.

check.q: What is a jijnasu?
check.why: A jijnasu is a seeker who wants to know.

check.q: How do the Upanishads treat questions?
choices: As a respected way to learn
check.why: The Upanishads present questioning as a path to knowledge.

lessons.title: Gargi at the King's Court
lessons.mainIdea: In Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 3, Gargi Vachaknavi questions the sage Yajnavalkya in a public debate.
reading: King Janaka of Videha holds a great contest. He offers a thousand cows, their horns tied with gold, to the wisest scholar. The sage *Yajnavalkya* tells his student to lead the cows away. The other scholars challenge him.
Among them is *Gargi* Vachaknavi. She asks what the world is woven on, like cloth on a loom. Each time he answers, she asks what that is woven on, and so on. Yajnavalkya warns her not to ask too far.

Later Gargi returns with two questions, which she compares to two sharp arrows. Yajnavalkya answers with the teaching of the imperishable. Gargi then tells the scholars no one will defeat him. Many readers see her as a model of fearless learning.

words.d: a woman scholar who questions Yajnavalkya in Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 3
a great sage and teacher in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad
a wise king of Videha who hosts debates in the Upanishads

look.title: Woven On What?
look.text: Gargi: What is water woven on? Yajnavalkya: On air. Gargi: And air? On the space between. And that? On the worlds of the gods... (Brihadaranyaka 3.6)
look.prompt: What is Gargi doing with her questions? Why might a teacher say, 'Do not ask too far'?

check.q: Who hosts the debate where Gargi speaks?
check.why: King Janaka of Videha holds the contest in Brihadaranyaka 3.

check.q: What does Gargi compare her two questions to?
check.why: In Brihadaranyaka 3.8 Gargi likens her questions to arrows.

check.q: Whom does Gargi question?
check.why: Gargi questions the sage Yajnavalkya.

lessons.title: Maitreyi's Question
lessons.mainIdea: In the Brihadaranyaka, Maitreyi asks Yajnavalkya what will make her immortal, and he teaches her about the self.
reading: Yajnavalkya is about to leave home to become a wandering seeker. He plans to divide his property between his two wives, Katyayani and *Maitreyi*. Maitreyi asks a question: if the whole earth full of wealth were mine, would it make me immortal?
Yajnavalkya says no. Wealth brings only a wealthy life. Maitreyi answers: then what use is it to me? Tell me what you know. Pleased with her question, he agrees to teach her about the self.

He says that a husband, a wife, children and wealth are dear not for their own sake but for the sake of the self. The self must be seen, heard and reflected on. This dialogue appears twice, in chapters 2 and 4.

words.d: a wife of Yajnavalkya who asks him about immortality in the Brihadaranyaka
never dying

look.title: What Use Is Wealth?
look.text: Maitreyi asks: if this whole earth full of wealth were mine, would I become immortal by it? Yajnavalkya answers: no; your life would be like the life of rich people, but there is no hope of immortality through wealth.
look.cite: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.4.2, paraphrased (see F. Max Müller, SBE 15, 1884)
look.prompt: What does Maitreyi choose instead of wealth? How is her choice like Nachiketa's?

check.q: What does Maitreyi ask Yajnavalkya?
choices: Whether wealth will make her immortal
check.why: Maitreyi asks if the whole earth's wealth would make her immortal.

check.q: How is Maitreyi like Nachiketa?
choices: Both turn down wealth to seek knowledge
check.why: Each chooses teaching about the self over riches.

check.q: In which Upanishad is Maitreyi's dialogue?
check.why: The dialogue appears in Brihadaranyaka chapters 2 and 4.

lessons.title: Reading the Stories Today
lessons.mainIdea: Hindus and scholars today read the Upanishad stories as teachings about curiosity, honesty and who may learn.
reading: Many Hindu families tell Nachiketa's story to praise courage. Satyakama's story is told to praise honesty. Gargi and Maitreyi are often named as women philosophers from ancient India, and Indian schools and prizes carry Gargi's name.

Scholars add context. The stories come from a world where most teachers were men of priestly families. Gargi and Maitreyi stand out partly because they are rare in the texts. Scholars debate how much the stories reflect real history.
Still, the pattern is clear. In the Upanishads, a good question can come from a boy, a servant's son or a woman. Many readers find in that pattern a lasting lesson about who has the right to ask.

words.d: the time, place and situation that help explain a text
a person who thinks carefully about big questions such as truth and the self

look.cite: Katha, Chandogya and Brihadaranyaka Upanishads (Müller, SBE 1 and 15)

check.q: What pattern do many readers see in these stories?
